finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header without any verification, so any client can impersonate a user with grants and delete or rename files they should not control.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified (views.py:11, load_user before_request)
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") then del STORE[fid] (views.py:17-18); is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") then f["name"] = ... (views.py:25-27)

trace.note: g.user set directly from request header, no signature, session or token check
ensure_allowed uses the spoofed g.user for the delete authorization decision
is_allowed returns true when action is in grants[user]; user is attacker-chosen
file is deleted after the spoofed check passes
rename path uses the same spoofed g.user for the write check
name overwritten after the spoofed check passes

finding.guards_checked: before_request performs no validation of the header; authorization check is on the same object acted on; ensure_allowed and rename_file return 403 on denial; absent header gives g.user=None which yields an empty grant list. No trusted-proxy or header-stripping config exists in the repo, so exploitability depends on deployment: if a gateway always overwrites this header, risk drops.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. views.py:11 sets g.user straight from the request header with no verification. acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed does abort(403) on denial, and views.py:25 checks is_allowed's bool, but both only compare against the spoofed identity. acl.py:5 returns False for a missing header (grants.get(None) is empty), so an absent header is not a bypass. No gateway or header-stripping config exists in the repo.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 trusts X-Session-User-Verified as the caller identity, and views.py:17-18 and views.py:25-27 then authorize delete and rename against that identity via acl.py:5, so any client that can reach the app and knows a user with grants can act as that user. The residual risk is deployment-dependent: if an upstream proxy always strips or overwrites this header, the code-level flaw is not exposed, but nothing in the repo shows such a proxy.
